title: Lumen Candle Company: variable vs absorption costing and a production bonus
participant_role: Cost accountant for Lumen Candle Company explaining variable and absorption costing to the plant manager
judge_role: Plant manager of Lumen Candle Company, paid a bonus on absorption costing income, who plans to produce as much as possible next year

difficulty.rationale: Variable vs absorption income statements and reconciliation.

scenario:
You are to assume the role of a cost accountant for LUMEN CANDLE COMPANY, a manufacturer of scented soy candles. The plant manager (judge) has asked you to explain how the company calculates product costs and operating income and to review the plant manager's (judge's) production plan for next year.

LUMEN CANDLE COMPANY has just completed its first year of operations, so there was no beginning inventory. During the year, the plant produced 10,000 candles and sold 8,000 candles at $15 each. The remaining 2,000 candles are in finished goods inventory. The cost information for the year is shown below.

The plant manager (judge) earns an annual bonus equal to 10% of operating income as reported under absorption costing, the method used in the company's financial statements. After reviewing the first year results, the plant manager (judge) told you, "My plan for next year is simple: we produce as much as possible. The more candles we make, the lower our cost per candle and the higher our profit." The owners of the company have asked you to make sure the plant manager (judge) understands how the numbers work before next year's production schedule is set. The plant manager (judge) is an expert in candle making but has little accounting background.

You will meet with the plant manager (judge) to:
• Distinguish between variable costing and absorption costing
• Calculate the unit product cost and the cost of goods sold under each method
• Prepare an income statement under each method
• Explain why operating income is different under the two methods
• Explain the ethical concerns with producing extra inventory to increase the bonus and recommend a better performance measure

You will present your information to the plant manager (judge) in a role-play to take place in the plant manager's (judge's) office. The plant manager (judge) will begin the role-play by greeting you and asking to hear your ideas. After you have presented your information and have answered the plant manager's (judge's) questions, the plant manager (judge) will conclude the role-play by thanking you for your work.

judge_questions: It's legal to produce more candles. Why is it wrong?
Which method must we use for our bank and our tax return?

solution.overview: A strong answer explains that absorption costing puts fixed manufacturing overhead into each candle while variable costing expenses it in the period, then shows absorption operating income of $22,000 versus variable costing operating income of $14,000. The presenter reconciles the $8,000 difference to the $4 of fixed overhead carried in each of the 2,000 unsold candles, explains that overproducing inflates the bonus without creating real profit, and recommends a bonus measure that cannot be raised by building inventory.

answer: Absorption costing (full costing): product cost = direct materials + direct labor + variable overhead + fixed manufacturing overhead
Variable costing (direct costing): product cost = direct materials + direct labor + variable overhead only; fixed manufacturing overhead is expensed in full as a period cost
Selling and administrative costs are period costs under both methods
Direct costs (materials, labor) trace to each candle; overhead is an indirect cost that must be allocated
Absorption is required for external reports; variable costing is used inside the company for decisions
Fixed overhead per candle = $40,000 / 10,000 produced = $4
Absorption unit cost = $6 + $4 = $10; COGS = 8,000 x $10 = $80,000
Variable unit cost = $6; variable COGS = 8,000 x $6 = $48,000 (plus all $40,000 fixed overhead expensed as a period cost)
Ending inventory: absorption 2,000 x $10 = $20,000; variable 2,000 x $6 = $12,000
Absorption: Sales $120,000, COGS $80,000, gross profit $40,000, selling and administrative $18,000, operating income $22,000
Variable: Sales $120,000, variable costs $56,000, contribution margin $64,000, fixed costs $50,000, operating income $14,000
Same sales, same total spending; only the timing of fixed overhead expense differs
2,000 candles in ending inventory x $4 fixed overhead each = $8,000 deferred on the balance sheet under absorption costing
When production is greater than sales, absorption income is higher; when sales equal production, both methods give the same income
If only 8,000 candles were made: fixed overhead $5 per candle, COGS 8,000 x $11 = $88,000, absorption income $14,000 (same as variable)
Bonus: 10% x $22,000 = $2,200 under absorption vs 10% x $14,000 = $1,400 under variable, an $800 gain without selling one more candle
Overproducing uses cash, adds storage and handling costs, and risks obsolescence as scents go out of style
It is legal, but it puts the manager's bonus ahead of the owners' interests and makes reported profit misleading
Base the bonus on variable costing income (or sales and contribution margin) so it only rises when candles are sold
Add limits or targets: cap inventory growth, track inventory turnover and cash flow

judge_question_answers.question: It's legal to produce more candles. Why is it wrong?
answer: Legal is not the same as ethical: the extra profit comes from moving $8,000 of cost onto the balance sheet, not from selling more
It raises your bonus at the owners' expense and uses cash that is tied up in unsold candles
Extra inventory adds storage costs and may never sell, so a write-down later would erase the gain
Acting in the company's best interest and reporting honestly is what builds trust with the owners

judge_question_answers.question: Which method must we use for our bank and our tax return?
answer: Absorption costing is required for GAAP financial statements given to the bank and for the tax return
Variable costing is not allowed for external reporting, but it is a better tool for internal decisions and evaluating managers
Many companies keep both: absorption for outside reports, variable for inside management reports

key_concepts.definition: A costing method that includes all manufacturing costs, both variable and fixed, in the cost of each unit. Unit cost = direct materials + direct labor + variable overhead + fixed overhead per unit.
A costing method that includes only variable manufacturing costs in the cost of each unit and expenses all fixed manufacturing overhead in the period it occurs.
A cost attached to inventory that becomes an expense (cost of goods sold) only when the item is sold.
A cost expensed in the period it occurs, such as selling and administrative costs, no matter how many units are sold.
A direct cost can be traced to one product (materials, labor). An indirect cost, like factory overhead, is shared and must be allocated to products.

Factory costs that stay the same in total no matter how many units are made, such as rent or supervisor salaries. Fixed cost per unit = total fixed overhead / units produced, so it falls as production rises.
The cost of the units actually sold during the period. COGS = beginning inventory + cost of goods manufactured - ending inventory, or units sold x unit product cost.
Sales minus all variable costs; the amount left to cover fixed costs and profit. Contribution margin = sales - variable costs.
Sales minus cost of goods sold; used on an absorption costing income statement.
Absorption income - variable income = fixed overhead per unit x (units produced - units sold). When production is greater than sales, absorption income is higher.
How many times inventory is sold and replaced in a period. Inventory turnover = cost of goods sold / average inventory; a falling turnover can reveal overproduction.

notes: State level because students must build two full income statements, reconcile them, and connect the numbers to an incentive problem, all in 10 minutes. Watch for students who treat fixed selling and administrative cost as a product cost, who divide fixed overhead by units sold instead of units produced, or who call overproduction illegal instead of explaining why it is unethical and misleading.

items.label: Distinguish between variable costing and absorption costing

criteria.exceeds: Explains that absorption costing puts the $40,000 of fixed manufacturing overhead into each candle while variable costing expenses it in the period, reconciles the $8,000 income difference to 2,000 unsold candles x $4, and shows that producing only 8,000 candles would make both methods equal at $14,000.
criteria.meets: Correctly explains that absorption costing includes fixed manufacturing overhead in product cost and variable costing treats it as a period cost, and explains that the $8,000 difference comes from fixed overhead held in ending inventory.
criteria.below: Describes the two methods only in general terms, or cannot explain why operating income differs.
criteria.little: Does not distinguish the methods, or describes them incorrectly.

items.label: Describe types of costs used in managerial accounting

criteria.exceeds: Classifies Lumen's costs clearly: direct materials $3 and direct labor $2 trace to each candle, overhead is an indirect cost that must be allocated, variable costs change with volume while the $40,000 and $10,000 fixed costs do not, and selling and administrative costs are period costs under both methods.
criteria.meets: Distinguishes product costs from period costs and fixed from variable costs, and correctly treats selling and administrative costs as period costs.
criteria.below: Names cost types but misclassifies one, for example treats the $10,000 fixed selling and administrative cost as a product cost.
criteria.little: Does not describe cost types, or the classifications are mostly wrong.

items.label: Explain the role of ethics in financial-information management

criteria.exceeds: Explains that overproducing raises absorption income and the bonus ($2,200 versus $1,400, an $800 gain) without selling one more candle, so reported profit becomes misleading, and that the extra inventory ties up cash, adds storage costs and risks obsolescence.
criteria.meets: Explains that producing extra inventory to raise the bonus makes reported profit misleading and puts the manager's interest ahead of the owners'.
criteria.below: Says overproduction is wrong but cannot explain how it affects the numbers, or calls it illegal instead of unethical and misleading.
criteria.little: Does not address the ethical concern, or supports producing as much as possible.

items.label: Calculate the cost of goods sold

criteria.exceeds: Calculates fixed overhead of $4 per candle ($40,000 / 10,000 produced), unit costs of $10 (absorption) and $6 (variable), COGS of $80,000 and $48,000, ending inventory of $20,000 and $12,000, and full income statements showing operating income of $22,000 and $14,000.
criteria.meets: Calculates absorption COGS of $80,000 (8,000 x $10) and variable COGS of $48,000 (8,000 x $6), and operating income of $22,000 and $14,000.
criteria.below: Gets only part of the calculation, for example divides fixed overhead by the 8,000 units sold or leaves out fixed selling and administrative costs.
criteria.little: Does not calculate unit cost or COGS, or the numbers are unrelated to the exhibit.

criteria.exceeds: Respectfully tells the plant manager the plan is not in the owners' interest and recommends basing the bonus on variable costing income (or sales and contribution margin), with limits such as capping inventory growth and tracking inventory turnover and cash flow.
criteria.meets: Honestly explains the problem with the plan and recommends a bonus measure that cannot be raised by building inventory, such as variable costing income.
criteria.below: Points out the problem but recommends no better measure, or softens the message so the issue is unclear.
criteria.little: Does not model ethical behavior, or helps the manager raise the bonus through overproduction.

items.label: Critical Thinking: Reason effectively and use systems thinking

criteria.exceeds: Connects production volume to fixed overhead per candle, inventory, operating income and the bonus, and shows that income rises under absorption costing whenever production is greater than sales.
criteria.meets: Reasons correctly from the exhibit data to the $8,000 difference and why the manager's plan raises reported profit.
criteria.below: Reaches a conclusion without showing the reasoning, or misses how production affects income.

items.label: Problem Solving: Make judgments and decisions and solve problems

criteria.exceeds: Gives a clear recommendation to set production based on expected sales and to change the bonus to a measure tied to sales, with inventory and cash flow targets.
criteria.meets: Makes a clear recommendation against overproducing and for a better bonus measure.
criteria.below: Hesitates, or gives a recommendation that is partly correct or not clearly stated.
criteria.little: Makes no recommendation, or agrees with the plan to produce as much as possible.

criteria.exceeds: Explains the two costing methods in plain language a candle expert with little accounting background can follow, in a logical order, with confident and professional delivery.
criteria.meets: Presents the unit costs, income statements, reconciliation and ethics issue clearly and in an organized way.
criteria.below: Presentation is hard to follow, relies on jargon, or skips steps.

items.label: Creativity and Innovation: Show evidence of creativity

criteria.exceeds: Uses an effective visual such as side by side income statements, or shows the check that producing only 8,000 candles gives $14,000 under both methods, making the effect of overproduction obvious.
criteria.meets: Organizes the information in a way that makes the two methods easy to compare.
criteria.below: Presents the facts with little effort to make them engaging or easy to follow.
criteria.little: Shows no evidence of creativity or original thought.

items.label: Overall impression and responses to the judge's questions

criteria.exceeds: Answers both questions correctly and confidently: legal is not the same as ethical, since the extra profit comes from moving $8,000 of cost to the balance sheet, raises the bonus at the owners' expense and may be erased by a later write-down; and absorption costing is required for the bank's GAAP statements and the tax return, while variable costing is a better internal tool.
criteria.meets: Answers both questions mostly correctly, including why overproduction is unethical even though legal and that absorption costing is required for external reports and taxes.
criteria.below: Answers only one question correctly, or gives vague answers without numbers.
criteria.little: Cannot answer the judge's questions, or says variable costing can be used for the bank or tax return.

key_points: Absorption costing includes fixed manufacturing overhead in product cost; variable costing expenses it as a period cost
Fixed overhead per candle = $40,000 / 10,000 produced = $4; unit cost $10 absorption versus $6 variable
Operating income: absorption $22,000 (sales $120,000, gross profit $40,000, selling and administrative $18,000); variable $14,000 (contribution margin $64,000, fixed costs $50,000)
Difference of $8,000 = 2,000 unsold candles x $4 of fixed overhead held in inventory
Bonus is $2,200 under absorption versus $1,400 under variable, an $800 gain from overproduction without extra sales
Recommend basing the bonus on variable costing income (or sales and contribution margin) with inventory and cash flow limits
Absorption costing is required for GAAP statements to the bank and the tax return
